The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design

48

Shares

6

3

38

As models evolve faster than silicon cycles, chip architects must balance flexible compute, data movement, and defense-in-depth security.

October 1st, 2026 -

By: Ann Mutschler

Key Takeaways:

Successful edge AI design requires prioritizing long-term architectural adaptability, memory bandwidth, and system-level efficiency over raw peak NPU TOPS.
The mismatch between fast-evolving AI models and long silicon development cycles makes hardware-software co-design and heterogeneous compute increasingly important.
Security must be built into the hardware from the start to protect against software supply chain risks, data breaches, and silent perceptual fault injection.

The rapid buildout of the edge is forcing chip architects and design teams to rethink how they add AI to vertical market applications. The fundamental challenge is a mismatch in timelines, because engineering teams must design for AI models, workloads, and deployment requirements that inevitably will shift long after silicon decisions are locked in.
Compounding this, real-world edge performance rarely depends on peak NPU TOPS. More often, it depends on memory bandwidth, latency, power budgets, security, and data movement. To keep pace with evolving models, architects are leaning heavily into flexibility — embracing heterogeneous compute, programmable data paths, expandable memory, secure field updates, and tight hardware-software co-design.
But flexibility alone isn’t enough. AI introduces broad attack vectors across models, data, keys, firmware, and inference pipelines, so robust security must be architected into hardware from day one. At the same time, fragmented toolchains across runtimes and frameworks make hardware-aware optimization just as important as raw compute.
This structural shift is redefining standard component boundaries.
“CPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to do more and more parallel processing,” observed Rob Fisher, senior director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “NPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to become more flexible, and the convergence point is with the CPU, NPU, and GPU in the middle. We’re finding more customers are trying to hedge their bets against the future than trying to squeeze out every last drop of performance today. That means we’re no longer just looking at a GPU you can slot in that just does GPU-like things. This has system-level impacts on the whole SoC.”
When designing edge applications with AI as a product feature, chip architects and design teams have many considerations. Hardware choices drive these broader architectural decisions, but the challenge reaches well beyond NPU TOPs.
“AI model performance depends on architectural details for memory, latency, power, and security,” said Eduardo Montanez, vice president and head of PSOC Edge MCUs & Edge AI Solutions for Infineon’s IoT, Compute & Wireless Business. This is why the company’s edge microcontrollers include memory expandability, a low-latency architecture, and energy efficiency to enable battery-powered applications at the edge. They also include security features that are designed to protect data and software IP.
AI applications at the edge are already challenging chip architects and design teams to keep up with rapid changes in models and workloads.
“As new networks are continually popping up, any solution needs to be programmable to accommodate new networks and ever-changing activation functions and corresponding data types,” said George Wall, product marketing group director at Cadence. “At the same time, there are hard performance requirements that must also be met.”
This makes hardware-software co-design increasingly important. “AI models, NPUs, memory hierarchy, and optimization techniques such as quantization, pruning, and distillation must be jointly optimized to achieve efficient deployment,” noted Niranjan Sitapure, group product manager for generative AI at Siemens EDA.
The entire pipeline also must be optimized, because success depends on sensor ingestion, data preprocessing, inference, post-processing, and ongoing model lifecycle management.
Ideally, chip architects and design teams would have a detailed view of what an edge application will do, including the models it will use, required performance, available memory, and power constraints, so they can design a chip for optimal PPA.
“Unfortunately, that isn’t reality,” said Paul Karazuba, vice president of marketing, Silicon IP at Rambus. “Even compressed, the chip design cycle will predate the release of any product that contains the chip by a year or more. During that time, it’s reasonable to assume the edge application will evolve, including changes to the underlying model(s) and perhaps the available memory and power. This application evolution forces chip designers to concentrate their efforts on creating chips that can adapt to changing requirements, including but not limited to a focus on moving data efficiently and securely.”
For others, AI acceleration isn’t the biggest challenge. What limits chip performance and efficiency may depend on the rest of the application.
“But architects and designers don’t design for that. They focus on neural network acceleration, claiming very high but theoretical TOPS numbers that no real application even comes close to achieving,” said Graham Gobieski, chief technology officer and co-founder of Efficient Computer. “In fact, in many real workloads (e.g., sensor fusion, autonomy), a majority of the application still runs on whatever general-purpose but very inefficient core exists on the SoC. The real opportunity to enable intelligent applications isn’t a faster NPU; it’s making the other 80% of the application as efficient as the AI portion.”
Beyond efficiency, edge AI applications add numerous design challenges.
Core design challenges
Performance depends on more than the compute capabilities of the programmable processor being used. “For example, memory bandwidth must be sufficient to keep the computational units fed with data, and the data needs to be in a location that is easily accessible by the processor,” explained Cadence’s Wall. “Otherwise, the computational elements will basically sit underutilized. Determining workload requirements is difficult because chip designers won’t necessarily have insight into the networks consumers will be running 3 or 5 years from now.”
This challenge is compounded by the fact that edge AI is fundamentally a constraint-driven design problem. “You are dealing with tight power budgets, limited memory, mixed sensor inputs, and latency expectations that users feel immediately. The architecture has to be efficient before it can be intelligent,” Rambus’ Karazuba said.
As AI models evolve rapidly, system architectures need memory scalability for large data sets and AI models, along with enough memory for the non-AI portions of a design.
“Also, the design must allow for end-to-end, secure provisioning and deployment, allowing for field updates without compromising valuable data and software IP,” Infineon’s Montanez noted.
Moving model weights and activations between DRAM and compute engines can consume more power than the AI computation itself. “AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles. New architectures, operators, and generative AI workloads emerge continuously, creating pressure for hardware platforms to remain adaptable,” Siemens’ Sitapure said. “For critical/high-risk applications, edge systems such as ADAS, industrial automation, and robotics require predictable latency, high reliability, and operation even with limited connectivity.”
While data movement can dominate performance and efficiency, other challenges may be overlooked. “The first is simple but challenging,” said Efficient Computer’s Gobieski. “The intelligence has to fit on the device. This means a lot of engineering goes into squeezing a neural network into on-device memory before any application code runs. The second has a standard answer that backfires. Splitting the application across an NPU, CPU, and DSP might seem like playing to each block’s strengths, but it complicates development by requiring many different toolchains, and it spends the savings moving data between them.”
Hardware teams also face non-negotiable physical constraints, especially strict low-power budgets. Thermal dissipation limits and battery constraints dictate computational efficiency, along with demanding reliability requirements for mission- and safety-critical edge deployments, Sylvain Guilley, co-founder and chief technology officer at Secure-IC, a Cadence company, noted. “Solving these core challenges requires moving beyond proprietary, siloed hardware tricks toward broader industry-wide alignment on architectural standards. To build standard open framework specifications for edge hardware, Cadence is tackling this in a new OCP FCSA Sub-Project Workstream.”
Security from the start
Electronics developers looking to add AI to edge devices should incorporate several security technologies from the beginning of system design.
The starting point is a secure platform, followed by a secure application. “A secure platform is fundamental,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management for security solutions at Synopsys. “It establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy. Developers must still address authorization, data protection, output validation, connected-service security, and component assurance at the application layer. Assume the AI platform already provides a root of trust, secure boot, attestation, encrypted communications, and trusted execution environments. That establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy.”
At the application layer, Neustadter said developers must address additional controls, including:

Authorization: Ensure that only approved users and services can perform sensitive actions.
Data protection: Handle sensitive information appropriately throughout its lifecycle.
Output validation: Check AI results before they drive decisions or physical actions.
API and cloud security: Protect connected services, even though edge deployments place greater emphasis on the device itself.
Model and component assurance: Verify models, AI engines, plugins, and other third-party components before deployment.

A common misconception is that an AI result must be trustworthy simply because the AI runs on a secure platform. Consider a mobile robot whose model reports that a hallway is empty. If the software accepts that result without further checks, the robot could move and collide with an unexpected obstacle. “The AI provides an input to the decision. It should not be the sole basis for the final decision,” Neustadter explained. “The application should evaluate the model’s confidence score and complete additional checks before authorizing an action. It should also apply relevant rules and safety policies and confirm the environment before the device acts.”
Establishing a resilient platform also does not guarantee privacy. Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. For example, a smart camera in a mall may analyze shopper behavior. Even if the device is secure, storing those analytics in an unencrypted database could let an attacker access private customer information.
“Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. Developers should encrypt sensitive data and enforce access controls throughout its lifecycle. They should also retain data only as long as necessary and limit its use to authorized people and services,” she said.
Models should also be authenticated with controls comparable to secure boot. Before loading a model, the system should verify its identity, integrity, signature, and provenance. This is another reason a strong root of trust is essential. “Model confidentiality and access control should also be incorporated into the system’s key-management strategy,” Neustadter explained.
Edge AI systems may require additional keys. A third-party model provider, for example, may want to prevent the device owner or other parties from accessing the model without authorization. Model confidentiality and access control, therefore, become part of the overall key-management strategy.
All models and components can introduce software supply-chain risks. Developers often rely on open-source models, AI engines, plugins, and other external components. A model that contains a hidden backdoor can generate incorrect or malicious outputs, and secure hardware may still execute it if the system accepts the model as trusted.
“Secure hardware will still execute a compromised model if the system accepts it as trusted. To reduce the risk, developers should therefore verify provenance and integrity, validate suppliers, use trusted repositories, and maintain software bills of materials,” Neustadter added.
When designing security into edge applications and mitigating attack vectors introduced by AI, engineering leadership should involve high-level product management as early as possible. That allows developers to perform risk analysis and determine where mitigations are needed across both hardware interfaces and software layers, Cadence’s Guilley said.
“This early architectural grounding directly informs overall device strategy in terms of cyber-resiliency,” he noted. [“Establishing this foundation early] allows us to treat cybersecurity not as a cost but as an investment that enables subsequent operations to unfold safely 24/7 and to turn incidents away from emergencies and rather have them be seen as a business continuity plan.”
This unified security and governance framework becomes especially important when engineering complex cyber-physical systems that must comply with cybersecurity, AI, and data privacy mandates.
“Design teams must continuously navigate strict regulatory boundaries, specifically around the E.U. Cyber Resilience Act, statutory requirements concerning capturing personal data in personally identifiable information, and the overarching statutory mandates enforced under the broader E.U. AI Act,” Guilley said.
A root of trust and separation between secure and non-secure code are also important. “Having a bootloader that manages code authentication is critical,” Infineon’s Montanez said. “With AI moving to the edge, most products still have a hybrid approach with the cloud, allowing for OTA or other communication. Therefore, edge AI applications can require additional security for the connectivity link.”
Big picture, security must be anchored in hardware, from secure boot and trusted firmware to protected keys, memory, and model assets. AI increases the stakes because models, inputs, and outputs can all have significant economic value.
“One should consider that economic value is not just the models themselves or the data inside those models, but also the financial and legal implications of a third party tampering with that data,” Karazuba noted.
Introducing AI into an edge device adds capabilities and features that were often unavailable in prior non-AI-enabled versions. “Device makers must design AI-enabled edge devices with a stronger security profile, given the increased financial and legal implications of a security breach,” he said.
Encryption is another key element, Siemens’ Sitapure said. Model weights, training data, and inference pipelines should be encrypted and protected from tampering, extraction, and unauthorized access.
Above all, security cannot be an afterthought. “Malicious actors could try to hack the underlying model weights and insert their own model that disrupts subsystem operation or exploits other security vulnerabilities in the system,” Cadence’s Wall said. “Fortunately, approaches range from localized encryption/decryption engines to a dedicated security island.”
More broadly, the most dangerous failure in edge AI is not a crash, but a live system that keeps operating while silently believing the wrong state. Real-time decisions increasingly depend on the integrity of on-device inference because edge AI is deployed in cameras, robotics, vehicles, and industrial systems that rely on NPUs, GPUs, and TPUs for performance and efficiency, but are not typically designed to ensure inference integrity under fault conditions.
In a recent white paper that includes the experimental block diagram and physical setup used for fault injection and measurement, Keysight security researchers showed that precisely timed fault injection (FI) can corrupt the output of a production-class edge AI pipeline without modifying firmware, model weights, software configuration, or input data. On a commercial Rockchip RK3568 platform running YOLOv5s_ReLU, most faults had no observable effect or only shifted confidence scores, but a smaller fraction induced missed detections, phantom objects, and rare high-confidence misclassifications while the system continued to operate normally. The impact can reach beyond individual inference errors. When corrupted detector outputs feed downstream tracking systems, even brief or low-probability errors can be filtered as transient noise, latched into persistent tracked objects, or amplified into denser and longer-lived false system states.
In the observed sequences, repeated, bounded faults transformed transient detector errors into sustained false perceptions that persisted beyond the original fault window. Once represented as system state, these errors can influence alerts, automation logic, and operator decisions while the platform appears healthy, which has implications for product teams. Here, traditional measures of resilience, such as uptime or fault recovery, may be insufficient for AI-driven systems. Resilience also must include inference integrity and the ability to prevent corrupted outputs from becoming trusted system state.
At the same time, decentralizing compute offers a foundational safety advantage in some applications, reducing how much sensitive information can leave the device. “Running inference on the device means sensitive data never travels, so there is no communication channel to intercept, and decentralized processing means there is no central repository of sensitive data to breach,” Efficient Computer’s Gobieski said. “A compromise costs you one device, not the fleet. The model itself carries the usual concerns about what it exposes, but those are far smaller than the ones you eliminate by keeping the data on the device.”
Conclusion
Navigating the edge AI landscape requires a mindset shift for engineering teams. Success no longer hinges just on maximizing theoretical peak compute, but on balancing silicon longevity with rapid software evolution. By prioritizing flexible architectures, hardware-software co-design, and defense-in-depth security from day one, chip designers can build resilient platforms that adapt to whatever AI workloads emerge — even after the chip architecture is finalized.
